findings.passage: That line does more work than any other in the Seven reading.
findings.problem: The article's central discriminator does not stand up when the quote is read in context. The quote gives its own reason: shifts went away "because I didn't have much overhead" (VF 2017, said to explain why he happened to be working the day Rae Dawn Chong walked in). The same VF passage says he "threw himself into entertaining tables" and won "Gumper of the year" with "my name on a plaque". That fits a Three repairing worth in a new arena. Cohen's narration calls him "lost" in Maui, and after Henry he "surprised my friends by declaring that I was going to change my life." The move was not his chosen next step: by his 2026 telling, a friend saw that he looked "off" and bought him a one-way ticket. A depressed 19-year-old drifting after a failure fits several types, and it is also the Three's stress pattern of disengagement. The article says "he spent it on a beach" and that "No camera was on him", but it never confronts any of this. The FAQ answer to "Is Chris Pratt a Type 3?" repeats the problem ("he partied, then moved to Maui and gave away his restaurant shifts").
findings.acceptance_test: Near this passage, the article gives his stated low-overhead reason, the friend's rescue ticket and the Gumper award read as a possible Three move, then names what in the Maui record only a Seven predicts (for example the 2014 recasting of homelessness as "a charming time"). If it cannot, it downgrades the claim from "more work than any other" to one fit among several. The Type 3 FAQ no longer presents the move to Maui as his own choice after partying.

findings.passage: Read together, those lines describe a Seven's mask. The cheerful front was there to show people he "was okay," which is a claim about pain.
findings.problem: In the GQ context (reopened from the saved raw copy), Pratt frames the front as a matter of self-doubt and self-acceptance, not pain. The act was "a super-happy fat sweaty guy who is completely confident and accepting of who he was", and audiences wondered "Why is this guy not crippled with self-doubt?" GQ's paraphrase "didn't feel too great about who I was" concerns worth, and the evidence record's own `against` field lists it as the Three's worth-level clue. Yet this paragraph counts it as Seven support. "That image that I was casting, to convince people that I was okay" describes image management in plain terms. "Which is a claim about pain" is the author's gloss, presented as if it were what his words mean.
findings.acceptance_test: The paragraph says that an image cast to convince people, plus a self-judgment about "who I was", is the rival's natural reading. It then either gives a discriminator that only the Seven reading predicts (for example the "pure euphoria" eating loop as the payoff in itself) or says the mask fits both types. "Which is a claim about pain" is marked as inference ("this suggests") or removed.

findings.passage: Third, what he wants from a role. A Three wants top billing. Asked about Andy in 2026, Pratt said what he loved was "being a jazz soloist, but not the lead singer."
findings.problem: One of the three named tipping points rests on a stated preference that the article's own biography contradicts. The draft says he "became a leading man" in Guardians and Jurassic World. It also says he remade his body after Moneyball and "had always wanted to play an action hero", then led The Terminal List and Mercy. The jazz line (The Playlist, 2026-10-22) is about the "freedom" and "easy work" of a supporting part. It came in a promotional interview, in the same answer as "people really responded well to it", while he discussed a possible Schur project. It speaks to workload and play more than to billing. The same section spins the most disciplined, career-driven behavior in the record: "The diet traded a smaller pleasure for a bigger adventure" recasts years of dieting for the roles that paid as Seven appetite.
findings.acceptance_test: Either "top billing" is dropped as a tipping point, or the passage weighs it against a decade of lead roles and gives the quote's promotional context in the prose. The diet sentence sets the Three reading (body remade for the roles the market offered) beside the "adventure" gloss, or is marked as the author's interpretation.

findings.passage: Eleven years later he wants the fun back, and he has said what made it easy. The funny guy didn't have to be hurt.
findings.problem: The closing insight rests on two weak links. (1) Schur's "main character dilemma" is a screenwriting idea about character arcs: "They need to have a full arc. They need to grow. They need to learn. They need to be vulnerable. They need to be hurt" (The Playlist, 2026-10-22). The draft quotes only the last two sentences, and the closing line turns a craft point about Andy into a claim about Pratt's own avoidance of hurt, which he never made. (2) The comedy pivot came from "a meeting with my manager and agent" (Not Dead Yet, published 2026-03-31), about two months after Mercy (released 2026-01-23). Wikipedia calls Mercy "a critical and commercial failure" (src-wikipedia; the evidence record also logs src-numbers-mercy-2026). The article names Mercy only as "the January thriller Mercy", so readers cannot weigh the obvious market-repositioning reading. In the same answer he also said he now cares more about being "close to home". The fun he said he cast as an image in 2015 is also not the same thing as comedy roles in 2026.
findings.acceptance_test: The ending makes clear that "need to be hurt" describes a lead character's arc, and does not imply Pratt said he avoids being hurt. The final section states Mercy's reception with a date and source, and sets the market and family readings beside the Seven reading. The closing claim must survive both, or it is reframed as one reading.

findings.passage: His road rage lasted one clause.
findings.problem: This is a context-fidelity error inside the Eight rebuttal. In GQ (2015) the anger itself was not brief. He says he told himself "Just get mad. Just get fucking pissed", treated it as "great research" for his acting, and was "so pissed" through a detour that "cost me twenty minutes". Only the retelling flipped within one answer. The earlier line ("The anger lasted one clause before he talked himself out of it") has the same blur, and neither passage mentions that the anger was deliberately stoked as an acting exercise. That context does fit his separate 2026 remark that anger is "something that I don't do authentically very well". But the article states the duration of the event inaccurately.
findings.acceptance_test: Both road-rage passages describe the episode accurately: he whipped up the anger on purpose as acting research, it lasted the drive, and his blame reversed within one answer when he retold it to GQ. The Eight rebuttal no longer says his road rage lasted one clause.

findings.passage: A reader can still argue Three. The argument here is that Three explains the selling, and Seven explains the choices.
findings.problem: The summary line is contradicted by the article's own evidence. By his own account, he spent the years before 2018 "completely deferential to whatever the world wants. I'll give you literally anything. Just keep me employed as an actor" (Not Dead Yet, 2026). That is a repeated, costly choice, and the most direct Three line in the record. None of the three tipping points answers it. The article also records audience-tuned retellings ("Press tours tune a story to the room"; Maui told three ways; "His account has shifted with the setting"), plus Gunn's "didn't trust himself to just be Chris Pratt". It treats all of this as noise rather than weighing it as Three evidence. The Nine section reuses "the deference" without resolving it for Three.
findings.acceptance_test: "Why not Type 3?" answers the deference line and the pattern of audience-tuned retelling directly. For example, it can show what he says he was protecting (employment and money, or image and worth) and why the Seven reading explains it better. Otherwise it lists them as unexplained, and the summary sentence no longer claims Seven alone explains "the choices".

findings.passage: A sensitive boy, a father who treated sensitivity as a danger, and a clown built to keep the hurt out: that is the Seven's oldest defense, told in his own words.
findings.problem: Humor as a shield against a harsh father is cross-type; the evidence record's own alternative for c-humor-defense names 2, 3, 7 and 9. The sentence presents it as type-specific. The same GQ childhood answer adds "if I got yelled at, I would stay silent for a long period of time", a withdrawal response the article omits before claiming in the Nine section that Pratt does not go quiet. Other generic material gets the same Seven label: "His faith began in the Seven pattern" (broken altar promises) and "That is the Seven's trap, described from the inside" (the hole only God can fill, a stock evangelical testimony image).
findings.acceptance_test: Each of these three sentences uses fit language ("fits", "is consistent with") and either names what in the account is specifically Seven or admits that other types tell the same story. The Nine section does not imply he never goes quiet unless it addresses the childhood silence.

findings.passage: But a Six scans for danger and doubts first. Pratt hands that job to others: his manager is "calculated and critical in a way that I'm not."
findings.problem: Handing vigilance to a trusted authority is itself a recognized Six strategy, and the article's own Six evidence fits it: his brother redirected him from the army and into the photo, and his manager has him turn down "huge checks". So this sentence reads a Six marker as anti-Six. "Zero critical thinking skills were ever taught to anyone in my household" describes his family's naivety, not his level of anxiety. The one anecdote left ("should've made me nervous but didn't") is a conversion story told in hindsight.
findings.acceptance_test: The Six paragraph treats reliance on trusted guides as Six-consistent. It then gives a discriminator that separates the two types, such as a sourced example showing that pleasure or possibility, not anxiety, drives a costly choice. Otherwise it softens the rebuttal to a lean.

protected_passages.passage: People of every type hide a failure, so the hiding settles little.
protected_passages.reason: Honestly gives away the cheap evidence before arguing the type; keep this calibration.

protected_passages.passage: The limits are real. Most of the Seven evidence is his own retelling in interviews, the cleanest test came when he was about 19, and the "pure euphoria" line comes from auto-captions of a podcast.
protected_passages.reason: States the inference limits in the body, at the type argument, instead of hiding them in a footer.

protected_passages.passage: He has told that stretch three ways, from "a pretty awesome place to be homeless" in 2014 to a rescue from "the wrong path" in 2026. Press tours tune a story to the room.
protected_passages.reason: Shows readers that the anchor anecdote is a retold story; rare, valuable source skepticism.

protected_passages.passage: Even the commitment has a Seven texture. He got through the whole Bible by listening on Hallow, he said, because when he reads books like Leviticus, "my brain starts wandering four seconds in."
protected_passages.reason: A specific, surprising, sourced detail that complicates the faith section without overclaiming.

protected_passages.passage: Even so, more than a decade of public faith, held through the mockery, is the strand of Pratt the type explains least.
protected_passages.reason: Faces the strongest adverse evidence directly; protect this admission through edits.

assessment: The critic's question: does the Seven case confront the evidence against it, and are its causal stories supported? Partly. The draft is unusually honest in places: it gives away the hiding, states its limits and names faith as unexplained. But most of the alternatives sit in the evidence sidecar's `alternative` fields, not in the prose next to the claims they weaken. Opening the saved copies of GQ 2015, Vanity Fair 2017, the Not Dead Yet Whisper transcript and The Playlist 2026 shows that the four most attractive moves overread their sources. First, Maui is called the decisive test, but the quote's own reason is low overhead, he won an award at the same job and a friend bought the ticket. Second, the 'Seven's mask' paragraph counts self-doubt and image-casting, which are the rival's evidence, as Seven support. Third, 'A Three wants top billing' runs against a decade of lead roles. Fourth, the ending turns Schur's character-arc idea into a claim about Pratt's psyche and omits Mercy's failure before the comedy pivot. The Eight rebuttal also misstates the GQ road-rage episode, and the deference decade is never answered. Seven may still be the better read: the euphoria loop, mind-wandering and 'next ticket' lines are real. But the article claims a cleaner win than the record supports. Keep confidence at medium in the prose and let the rival land some blows. Similarity: the trip comes from self-matches with this page's own 2026-10-29 version, not reuse from other subjects. The only cross-subject overlaps are triad-orientation lines shared with Florence Pugh and 'gets a full hearing below' shared with Dominic Fike, which is ordinary type vocabulary, so no finding. Risk flags: sensitive allegations (the Hillsong/Zoe reporting and the Daily Beast 'lying' headline), contested typing (a retype from 3 to 7 whose discriminator is weaker than presented) and a major thesis change. No historical source uncertainty. I did not reopen the Club Random, SmartLess, Happy Sad Confused or Christian Post sources.
